component: English ASR + VAD + semantic turn-taking (streaming, Apple Silicon)
recommendation:
Three models, all local, all measured on this exact machine (Apple M5 Max, 40-core GPU, 128 GB, macOS 26.5.2):

1. ASR — **Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B** run through **mlx-qwen3-asr 0.4.0** (pure MLX, Apache-2.0, no torch, no transformers). NOT transformers+MPS. Measured p50 on this Mac: 90 ms (1.4 s utterance), 321 ms (3.9 s), 413 ms (6.3 s), 694 ms (8.9 s); 4.08 GB resident / 8.16 GB transient peak. Call it offline once per turn on the VAD-delimited numpy buffer — do NOT use its streaming API for the final transcript (see risks).
2. VAD — **runanywhere/silero-vad-v5** `silero_vad.onnx` (2.3 MB, MIT) on onnxruntime 1.29 CPUExecutionProvider. Measured 0.139 ms per 32 ms frame = 0.43 % of one core.
3. Semantic endpointing — **pipecat-ai/smart-turn-v3**, file `smart-turn-v3.2-cpu.onnx` (8.7 MB int8, BSD-2). Measured 18.0 ms mean / 18.9 ms p95 on CPU with 4 intra-op threads.

Measured end-to-end "last speech sample → transcript in hand" with all three composed: **611 ms** for a 3.9 s utterance, **648 ms** for 6.3 s, **934 ms** for 8.9 s (200 ms VAD hangover + 46-64 ms endpoint compute + ASR). That leaves ~1.05-1.4 s of the 2.0 s target for LLM TTFT + TTS TTFA.

The user's ask is validated on both counts: silero-vad-v5 ONNX is the right VAD, and 1.7B (not 0.6B) is correct here — the author's 16 GB machine forced the downgrade, this one has 128 GB and 4.1 GB resident is nothing.
why:
**1.7B vs 0.6B.** The author's downgrade was a 16 GB decision, not an accuracy decision — he went back to 1.7B the moment he had a 4090 (docs/plan-4090.md). On this Mac the 1.7B costs 4.08 GB resident (3 % of 128 GB) and is only 130-234 ms slower than 0.6B per turn (measured: 321 vs 191 ms at 3.9 s; 694 vs 460 ms at 8.9 s). It buys 26 % relative WER on hard audio (LibriSpeech test-other 3.38 vs 4.55). Worth it. The `-hf` trap is real and I verified it structurally, but it does not apply on the MLX path — mlx-qwen3-asr reads the non-`-hf` repo on purpose and strips the `thinker.` prefix itself in convert.py.

**Accented English is the whole ballgame, and it is why Qwen3-ASR wins.** The Qwen3-ASR technical report's accented-English set (16 accent groups, dialog-style): Qwen3-ASR-1.7B **16.07** WER, 0.6B 16.62, Whisper-large-v3 **21.30**, GPT-4o-Transcribe 28.56. Qwen is 25 % relatively better than Whisper on exactly the population this user belongs to. Whisper-large-v3-turbo is a *pruned-decoder* variant of large-v3, so it sits at or below 21.30 — and its 30 s window puts a hard floor of ~1 s on caption latency. distil-whisper inherits the same accent weakness with no compensating advantage. Parakeet TDT is genuinely spectacular on speed (I measured 32/72/149/111 ms on the same four clips, RTF 0.012-0.023, 4-8× faster than Qwen 1.7B) and is competitive on *native* read English, but it is a transducer trained mostly on clean European-language speech and degrades on L2 accents (published: Japanese-accented 9.74 %, Russian 7.81 % vs <4 % for standard British/American), it has no context-biasing hook, and the Qwen paper's accented row has no Parakeet entry at all. For a non-native learner arguing at speed, robustness beats 300 ms.

**Why MLX and not transformers/MPS.** Nothing is installed on this box — going the transformers route means pulling torch (~2 GB) plus transformers plus an unproven MPS bf16 path for a brand-new multimodal architecture. mlx-qwen3-asr is a ground-up MLX reimplementation, quality-gated against the PyTorch reference (within 0.19 pp WER on AMI IHM + Earnings22, n=200), Metal-native, and I installed and ran it here in one command with zero friction. It also accepts a raw numpy float32 array, which is exactly what the VAD hands you — no file round-trip.

**Two-stage endpointing is the single biggest latency lever in this component.** Silero alone forces you to choose between a long hangover (600-800 ms of dead air on every turn) and cutting the user off mid-thought. SmartTurn lets you set the hangover to 200 ms and recover the mistakes semantically for 18 ms. That is a 400-600 ms saving on *every single turn*, for 0.43 % of one CPU core plus one 18 ms classification. VoxEMW's config pushes this to the extreme — `min_silence_ms: 64` — precisely because SmartTurn is doing the real deciding.

evidence.claim: Qwen3-ASR-1.7B is the best open model on accented English by a wide margin — 16.07 WER vs Whisper-large-v3's 21.30 and GPT-4o-Transcribe's 28.56
evidence.detail: Qwen3-ASR Technical Report (arXiv 2601.21337), robustness section: "Dialog-Accented English" averaged over 16 accent groups. Qwen3-ASR-1.7B 16.07, Qwen3-ASR-0.6B 16.62, Whisper-large-v3 21.30, GPT-4o-Transcribe 28.56. Report states Qwen3-ASR "achieves the lowest WER among all compared systems, surpassing both commercial APIs and open-source baselines, indicating better generalization to accent variation." Note the 1.7B/0.6B gap on THIS metric is only 0.55 pp — the 1.7B's real edge is elsewhere (test-other 3.38 vs 4.55).

evidence.claim: The non-'-hf' Qwen3-ASR repo really does use a thinker.* key layout that transformers 5.x cannot map — verified directly from the published weight index, not from the author's note
evidence.detail: Fetched https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B/resolve/main/model.safetensors.index.json: 708 weight keys, ALL prefixed `thinker.` — 397 under `thinker.audio_tower.*`, 310 under `thinker.model.*`, 1 `thinker.lm_head`. Its config.json nests everything under `thinker_config`, declares `transformers_version: 4.57.6`, and names the audio encoder `qwen3_asr_audio_encoder`. The -hf repo's config.json is flat (`audio_config` / `text_config` at top level), declares `transformers_version: 5.13.0.dev0`, and names the encoder `qwen3_asr_encoder`. Different model_type string + different key prefix = transformers loads without raising and leaves audio_tower/projector randomly initialised, exactly as VoxEMW trap #3 records. Corroborated independently by mlx-qwen3-asr's convert.py, whose docstring is literally "Strip 'thinker.' prefix from all keys / HF: thinker.audio_tower.conv2d1.weight -> audio_tower.conv2d1.weight". VERDICT: the author's trap is real. It does NOT apply to the MLX path, which handles the remap itself.

evidence.claim: MEASURED on this M5 Max: Qwen3-ASR-1.7B fp16 via MLX costs 90/321/413/694 ms (p50) for 1.4/3.9/6.3/8.9 s utterances, 4.08 GB resident
evidence.detail: mlx-qwen3-asr 0.4.0, mlx 0.32.2, macOS 26.5.2, in-memory float32 numpy input (file I/O excluded), language="English" forced, N=20 per clip, machine load average 8.6 (i.e. these are pessimistic). p50 / p90 / min: 1.4 s clip 90.4 / 136.5 / 82.3 ms; 3.9 s 321.1 / 784.0 / 247.3; 6.3 s 413.2 / 478.3 / 347.3; 8.9 s 694.1 / 942.6 / 645.9. mx.get_active_memory() 4.08 GB, mx.get_peak_memory() 8.16 GB. Cold start (weights load + first transcribe) 11.8 s — warm the process at boot. Same script, Qwen3-ASR-0.6B: 62.7 / 190.9 / 238.9 / 460.2 ms p50, 1.57 GB active / 3.14 GB peak. Transcripts were verbatim-correct on all four clips for both sizes.

evidence.claim: MEASURED on this M5 Max: full endpoint+ASR chain delivers a transcript 611-934 ms after the user's last speech sample
evidence.detail: Composed Silero VAD (7 hangover frames) + SmartTurn v3.2-cpu (1 call) + Qwen3-ASR-1.7B offline pass, N=6, p50: 3.9 s utterance = 200 ms real silence hangover + 63.5 ms endpoint compute + 347.2 ms ASR = 610.7 ms; 6.3 s = 200 + 50.8 + 397.1 = 647.9 ms; 8.9 s = 200 + 45.6 + 688.3 = 933.9 ms. Against a 2.0 s target this leaves 1.07-1.39 s for LLM TTFT + TTS TTFA; against the 3.0 s ceiling it is comfortable.

evidence.claim: MEASURED: Silero VAD v5 ONNX costs 0.139 ms per 32 ms frame on this Mac = 0.43 % of one core — but it silently returns ~0.001 for everything unless you prepend 64 samples of context
evidence.detail: runanywhere/silero-vad-v5 silero_vad.onnx (2.3 MB, MIT), onnxruntime 1.29.0 CPUExecutionProvider, intra_op_num_threads=1. Signature: input [B,N] float32, state [2,B,128] float32, sr int64 scalar; outputs prob [B,1] and stateN. GOTCHA I HIT: at 16 kHz you must feed 576 samples = the previous chunk's last 64 samples concatenated with 512 new samples. Feeding a bare 512-sample frame runs without error and returns ~0.001 on loud speech — a silent, total failure. With the context prepend it is exact: on a clip with 0.50 s silence + 3.89 s speech + 0.80 s silence it flagged speech from 0.51 s to 4.45 s (truth 0.50-4.39 s). Timing with the correct 576-sample input: mean 0.139 ms, p95 0.215 ms. The runanywhere README documents none of this.

evidence.claim: MEASURED: SmartTurn v3.2 int8 ONNX costs 18.0 ms mean / 18.9 ms p95 on this Mac's CPU — and CoreML EP makes it 3x WORSE, so use plain CPU
evidence.detail: smart-turn-v3.2-cpu.onnx (8.68 MB int8), realistic random input_features [1,80,800]. CPUExecutionProvider 4 threads: mean 18.00 ms, p50 17.90, p95 18.94. Single thread: 37.5 ms. CoreMLExecutionProvider: mean 56.72 ms, p95 88.49 — onnxruntime warns "number of partitions supported by CoreML: 43, number of nodes in the graph: 487, number of nodes supported by CoreML: 117", i.e. it shreds the graph into 43 partitions and thrashes on transfers. Corollary: VoxEMW's `_patch_smart_turn_gpu` monkeypatch in launch.py is dead code on Mac — delete it, don't port it.

evidence.claim: The smart-turn-v3 repo ships five checkpoints; v3.2-cpu is the one to use — 94.26 % English accuracy, FPR 3.75 %, FNR 1.99 %
evidence.detail: Per-checkpoint benchmark cards committed in the repo (benchmarks/*.md, 31,527 samples, 23 languages, generated 2026-01-07). English row (n=7,820) by checkpoint: v3.0 85.49 % acc / 8.41 FPR; v3.1-cpu 90.66 / 5.92; v3.1-gpu 91.94 / 5.82; v3.2-cpu 94.26 / 3.75; v3.2-gpu 94.71 / 2.98. The fp32 'gpu' file (32 MB) buys only +0.45 pp over the int8 'cpu' file (8.7 MB) and, per the measurement above, runs slower on this hardware. VoxEMW's README naming it 'v3.2' is correct and current.

evidence.claim: The two-stage design is documented by Pipecat exactly as VoxEMW uses it, and the payoff is a 0.2 s VAD hangover instead of ~0.8 s
evidence.detail: Pipecat docs: "Voice Activity Detection (using the Silero model) detects when there is a pause in the user's speech"; Smart Turn then analyses "the audio from the most recent 8 seconds of the user's turn." Recommended VAD `stop_secs` is 0.2 s ("which is the default value"), separate from the analyzer's own `stop_secs` (default 3.0 s) which is the give-up timer: "if a turn is classified as incomplete but silence continues for longer than stop_secs, the turn is automatically marked as complete." `pre_speech_ms` default 500 ms of pre-roll; `max_duration_secs` default 8.0 s with a rolling window beyond that. Model input is a 80x800 log-mel = 8 s at 10 ms hop (confirmed from the ONNX signature I read locally). VoxEMW pushes the VAD side to `min_silence_ms: 64` and lets SmartTurn arbitrate.

evidence.claim: The hotword hallucination trap is recorded twice in VoxEMW as a measured event, with the safe limit set at 2 words
evidence.detail: configs/assistant.yaml, stt.hotwords comment: "热词偏置（概率性，务必克制：词越多模型越容易把没说的话脑补成词表内容——2026-08-23 实测 10 个词时整段幻觉出词表。只留人设核心词 + corrections 兜底）" — with 10 hotwords, measured, the model hallucinated the whole vocabulary list into unrelated speech; he cut the list to 2 (`[魔镜女巫, 魔镜]`). He then built a runtime detector for it: voxemw/gateway/orchestrator.py `is_vocabulary_recitation()`, docstring "噪音/杂声被热词先验脑补成「良子，大胃袋，味真足。」这种整段词表复读（2026-08-23 实测出现）" — strip the hotwords longest-first from the transcript; if ≥2 matched and nothing is left over, it is a recitation, discard the turn. Deterministic post-hoc `corrections` (a plain string-replace table) is the zero-latency backstop he uses instead of more hotwords.

evidence.claim: Mechanism: Qwen3-ASR hotwords are decoder prompt context, not an acoustic-lattice bias — same failure mode as Whisper's initial_prompt
evidence.detail: The -hf model card puts the vocabulary in a system message ("Vocabulary: Quilter, apostle, gospel.") which becomes part of the autoregressive decoder's context; the technical report says only that "the model learns to utilize the context tokens inside the system prompt as background knowledge" and documents no limits or failure modes. Because the decoder is a Qwen3 LM doing next-token prediction over acoustic evidence + text context, a long vocabulary list raises the prior on those tokens AND presents itself as a fluent comma-separated sequence the LM can simply continue. When acoustic evidence is weak (silence, room noise, a filled pause, a clipped word) the prior dominates the likelihood and the model emits the list. This is the documented Whisper initial_prompt pathology — "a prompt can actually make hallucinations worse because the prompt text becomes context the decoder may repeat" — and Qwen3-ASR inherits it structurally. SAFE LIMIT: for an English debate partner, use ZERO hotwords; there is no persona jargon to protect and the downside is unbounded. If you must, ≤3 rare, acoustically distinctive proper nouns, plus a deterministic post-replace table and a recitation detector.

evidence.claim: VoxEMW's trap #4 (prompt= ignored, continue_final_message broken) is FIXED upstream — do not port his manual chat-template workaround
evidence.detail: I installed transformers 5.16.1 and read the source: `transformers.models.qwen3_asr.processing_qwen3_asr.Qwen3ASRProcessor.apply_transcription_request(audio, language=None, prompt=None, **kwargs)` exists, and its docstring reads "prompt (str or list[str], optional): Context/hotwords to include as the system prompt... When None, the system prompt is left empty." The -hf model card (chat-template PR merged 22 July) also now documents `continue_final_message=True` as the supported way to force language. His stt_qwen3asr.py hand-assembles the prompt string and appends "language Chinese<asr_text>" because 5.14 ignored `prompt=`; that code is obsolete. Irrelevant anyway on the MLX path, which exposes the same feature as `context="term1 term2"`.

evidence.claim: MEASURED head-to-head on the same four clips: Parakeet TDT 0.6b v3 via MLX is 4-8x faster than Qwen3-ASR-1.7B — the speed claim is real
evidence.detail: parakeet-mlx 0.5.2 with mlx-community/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3, in-memory mx.array, get_logmel + generate + mx.eval timed, N=15. p50: 1.4 s clip 32.1 ms (RTF 0.0229), 3.9 s 72.4 ms (0.0186), 6.3 s 148.6 ms (0.0234), 8.9 s 110.7 ms (0.0124). 1.30 GB active / 3.52 GB peak. Transcripts verbatim-correct including punctuation and the question mark Qwen dropped. It also has a real streaming API (`model.transcribe_stream(context_size=(256,256))`, 1 s chunks). This is the fallback if the latency budget collapses — but it is a CC-BY-4.0 25-European-language transducer with no context-biasing hook and no published accented-English number.

evidence.claim: Parakeet degrades on L2-accented English in a way Qwen3-ASR does not
evidence.detail: Published accent breakdown: "The Parakeet-TDT model shows significant variance across accents, with standard British and American English yielding low WERs (<4%), while heavily accented speech such as Japanese (9.74%) and Russian (7.81%) presents a much more complex challenge" — a 2-2.5x degradation. Parakeet-TDT-0.6b-v3's own card reports 6.34 % WER clean and 11.66 % at 0 dB SNR. Cross-check on the Qwen paper's English table: Parakeet-TDT-0.6B is competitive on clean read speech (LibriSpeech test-clean 1.93 vs Qwen-1.7B's 1.63, test-other 3.59 vs 3.38) but the paper's accented row simply has no Parakeet entry, and NVIDIA publishes none. This is weak-inference on the exact number, strong on the direction.

evidence.claim: Independent M5-class benchmark corroborates my numbers and shows Qwen3-ASR quantized is both more accurate AND lighter than WhisperKit turbo
evidence.detail: Soniqo benchmark on Apple M5 Pro / 48 GB / macOS 25.5, LibriSpeech test-clean first 200 utterances: Qwen3-ASR 1.7B 5-bit — 1.32 % WER, RTF 0.027, 1.92 GB peak RSS; Qwen3-ASR 1.7B 8-bit — 1.52 %, RTF 0.033, 2.7 GB; WhisperKit Large-v3 Turbo FP16 — 1.71 %, RTF 0.084; Parakeet TDT v3 INT8 — 2.37 %, RTF 0.009 (117.4x real time). So on an M5 Pro the quantized 1.7B is 3x faster than my fp16 measurement on M5 Max — quantization is the obvious headroom lever if I need it. mlx-qwen3-asr's own M4 Pro table says 8-bit g64 "reproduces fp16 output exactly on test-clean" at 1.32x speed; 4-bit costs +0.3 pp clean / +1.4 pp other at 1.71x.

evidence.claim: MEASURED: mlx-qwen3-asr's streaming API cuts the tail to ~140 ms but corrupts the text at chunk seams — do not use it for final transcripts
evidence.detail: init_streaming(chunk_size_sec=2.0) + 200 ms feeds + finish_streaming. finalization_mode="latency", enable_tail_refine=False gave a flat tail of 226.7 / 140.8 / 137.1 ms for 3.9 / 6.3 / 8.9 s clips — genuinely length-independent, which is exactly what you want. BUT the text came back duplicated at seams: "...for teenagers, because. Because education works better..." and "The point I am making is that. When you restrict access, you do not. Do not remove the demand." Same artifacts in "accuracy" mode. Also feed_audio() blocks the caller for up to 1151 ms on a chunk boundary, so it cannot sit on the audio thread. Offline transcription of the VAD-delimited buffer produced clean text every time. This matches VoxEMW's own architecture: stt_qwen3asr.py yields PartialTranscription for `mode == "progressive"` chunks with the comment that they are preview-only and "绝不能当最终转写 yield" — never yield them as the final transcript.

evidence.claim: Barge-in needs echo cancellation plus a transcript-level echo guard — VoxEMW ships both and the second one exists because the first is not sufficient
evidence.detail: AEC is the required first line: "Echo cancellation (AEC) removes the agent's outbound audio from the inbound signal so VAD only responds to genuine caller speech, not reflections of the agent itself", and "When both the user and the agent are speaking simultaneously (barge-in scenarios), AEC has the hardest job — it must cancel the echo while preserving the user's speech." VoxEMW ships a second line anyway: orchestrator.py `is_echo(user_transcript, recent_assistant)` — normalize away punctuation, require ≥4 chars, require a ≥4-char CONTIGUOUS match block AND ≥50 % total coverage against the last two assistant turns. His comment explains why the contiguity requirement was added after three false kills: "回声重放的是连续音频，必然带出长连续块；而真实短答只会撞上零散文案...2026-08-23 实测三轮误杀后加这道". On trigger he sets `_suppress_ghost` and discards every event of that turn. He also shipped iOS `voiceChat` AudioSession specifically for system-level AEC (v1.8.1 changelog).

evidence.claim: Backchannels ('yeah', 'right', 'mm-hm') are the dominant false-barge-in source in argumentative speech; the fix is a word-count gate, not a VAD threshold
evidence.detail: Pipecat: "By default, any user speech immediately interrupts the bot, but this can be problematic when users engage in backchanneling — brief vocal responses like 'yeah', 'okay', or 'mm-hmm' that indicate they're listening without intending to interrupt." Their answer is MinWordsInterruptionStrategy(min_words=3) (now `pipecat.turns.user.MinWordsUserTurnStartStrategy` via PipelineTask's `turn_start_strategies`). For a debate this matters more than for most apps — agreement/disagreement noises are constant. Two-tier policy: duck TTS gain on VAD speech_start (fast, reversible, ~50 ms), commit to full interrupt only once the ASR partial clears the word gate.

evidence.claim: On interrupt you must rewrite the assistant's context to what the user ACTUALLY heard, computed from samples played — not samples generated
evidence.detail: voxemw/gateway/audio_pacer.py tracks `_audio_samples_played` separately from `_audio_samples_fed` with the comment "打断回报估算「用户实际听到了多少」靠它而不是喂入时钟（TTS 生成快于播放 RTF<1，按喂入量算会高估）" — because TTS generates faster than real time (RTF < 1), counting fed samples over-estimates what was heard, sometimes by seconds. orchestrator.py then logs "打断回报：已播 %.1fs，已听前缀 %d 字补写回上下文" and writes that prefix back, because upstream rolls the whole reply out of context on interrupt. In a debate this is not cosmetic: if the AI thinks it made an argument the user never heard, it will reference it and the conversation desynchronises. Read `_audio_samples_played` BEFORE calling pacer.flush(), which zeroes the queue.

evidence.claim: Qwen3-ASR's streaming capability is architectural, not bolted on — dynamic 1-8 s attention windows, and streaming costs only ~0.3-1.1 pp WER
evidence.detail: Technical report: "Dynamic flash attention window size ranging from 1s to 8s, which allows Qwen3-ASR to perform both streaming inference with short chunks and offline inference with long queries." Streaming config is 2 s chunks, 5-token fallback, last four chunks unfixed. LibriSpeech degradation offline→streaming for the 1.7B: 1.63-3.38 % → 1.95-4.51 %. The -hf model card confirms "Both models support streaming/offline unified inference with a single model." Real config confirmed in the -hf config.json: `n_window: 50`, `n_window_infer: 800`, 24 encoder layers, d_model 1024, 128 mel bins, 28-layer Qwen3 decoder, hidden 2048, tie_word_embeddings true.

evidence.claim: This machine is the top M5 Max bin — 40-core GPU, 614 GB/s, 128 GB — so there is no memory pressure anywhere in this stack
evidence.detail: Verified locally: system_profiler reports Chip "Apple M5 Max", 18 CPU cores, 128 GB, GPU "Total Number of Cores: 40", Metal 4, macOS 26.5.2 (build 25F84). Apple's spec: M5 Max 32-core GPU = 460 GB/s, 40-core = 614 GB/s, each GPU core carries a Neural Accelerator (1,024 FP16 FMAs/cycle), >4x peak GPU AI compute vs M4 Pro/Max, plus a separate 16-core Neural Engine. The published mlx-qwen3-asr numbers are from an M4 Pro (273 GB/s), so this box has 2.25x the bandwidth. My measured latencies did NOT scale by 2.25x, which suggests MLX 0.32.2 is not yet exploiting the M5 Neural Accelerators for this workload — that is headroom, not a problem.

alternatives.name: Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B via mlx-qwen3-asr (the author's own Mac choice)
alternatives.tradeoff: Measured 1.4-1.5x faster on this Mac (63/191/239/460 ms p50 vs 90/321/413/694) and 2.6x lighter (1.57 GB vs 4.08 GB active). Costs only 0.55 pp on the accented-English benchmark (16.62 vs 16.07) — nearly a wash on the metric that matters most here. Costs more where audio gets hard: LibriSpeech test-other 4.55 vs 3.38 (+35 % relative), FLEURS multilingual 9.54 % vs 6.70 % primary error rate.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: If integration shows the 1.7B's p90 tail (784 ms on a 3.9 s clip, 943 ms on 8.9 s, measured under load) breaking the 2.0 s budget once a local LLM and TTS are contending for the same Metal device. Also the right call if you later want to run this on a smaller Mac. Swapping is a one-line model-path change — both are already downloaded.

alternatives.name: 8-bit quantized Qwen3-ASR-1.7B (mlx-qwen3-asr convert, group_size 64)
alternatives.tradeoff: Upstream reports 1.32x faster than fp16 with 8-bit reproducing fp16 output exactly on LibriSpeech test-clean; the independent M5 Pro run shows 5-bit at RTF 0.027 / 1.92 GB RSS, which is ~3x faster than my fp16 measurement. Cost is a conversion step (the quantize script lives in the GitHub repo, not the wheel) and unverified behaviour on accented speech specifically — all published quantization deltas are on clean read English.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: The first thing to try if you want 1.7B accuracy at closer to 0.6B latency. Do it only after you have a held-out set of the user's own accented speech to verify the quantization does not cost more on accented audio than it does on LibriSpeech.

alternatives.name: NVIDIA Parakeet TDT 0.6b v3 via parakeet-mlx 0.5.2
alternatives.tradeoff: Measured 4-8x faster on this exact machine (32/72/149/111 ms p50, RTF 0.012-0.023, 1.30 GB active) with a real streaming API and better punctuation than Qwen on my clips. Loses on the one axis that decides this: L2-accented English (published <4 % native vs 9.74 % Japanese-accented, 7.81 % Russian-accented). Also no context-biasing hook, CC-BY-4.0 rather than Apache-2.0, and 25 European languages only.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: If the LLM turns out to be far slower than expected and ASR has to fit in ~150 ms, or as a cheap parallel draft transcript for on-screen interim text and the barge-in word-gate while Qwen produces the authoritative final. Also the right pick if you later discover the user's accent is mild enough that Qwen's edge does not show up in practice — test, don't assume.

alternatives.name: whisper-large-v3-turbo via mlx-whisper or WhisperKit
alternatives.tradeoff: Worse on exactly the target population: Whisper-large-v3 is 21.30 WER on the accented set vs Qwen 1.7B's 16.07, and turbo is a pruned-decoder derivative that trades accuracy for speed, so it sits at or below that. Its 30 s processing window imposes a caption-latency floor "of a second or more", versus Parakeet's "low hundreds of milliseconds". Its one unique capability is speech translation, which a monolingual English debate partner does not need.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Only if you later want the AI to accept the user's native language mid-turn and translate. For pure accented-English recognition there is no configuration in which this beats Qwen3-ASR here.

alternatives.name: distil-whisper (English-only distilled Whisper)
alternatives.tradeoff: Inherits Whisper's accent weakness with a smaller model, so accuracy on L2 English is worse than large-v3's 21.30, while still being slower than Parakeet and less accurate than Qwen. It is dominated on both axes simultaneously.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: Never, for this use case. Listed only to close it off explicitly — it was on the candidate list and it should come off.

alternatives.name: FluidAudio (Swift/CoreML on the Apple Neural Engine) — Parakeet EOU 120m or Nemotron streaming 0.6b
alternatives.tradeoff: Runs entirely on the ANE, "minimizing CPU usage and avoiding GPU/MPS entirely" — which means ASR stops competing with a local LLM and TTS for the Metal device, the single biggest systemic risk in this design. Parakeet EOU 120m is streaming ASR *with end-of-utterance detection built into the same model*, ~232 MB, and would collapse VAD+SmartTurn+ASR into one component; shipping apps report ~0.13 s latency. Cost: it is a Swift SDK, so it does not drop into a Python pipeline, and Parakeet EOU is English-only with Parakeet's accent profile.
alternatives.when_to_prefer: If you build the app natively in Swift rather than Python, or if GPU contention between ASR, a local LLM and TTS turns out to be the real bottleneck. Worth benchmarking before committing to a Python architecture, because the architectural win (ASR off the GPU entirely) is larger than any per-model latency difference in this whole report.

latency_estimate:
MEASURED on this machine, not estimated. All figures p50, machine under real load (load average 8.6), so treat them as pessimistic.

Per-stage, from the user's last speech sample:
- VAD hangover — 200 ms of real silence (a policy choice, not compute). This is the number SmartTurn lets you shrink; without it you would need 600-800 ms.
- VAD compute over the hangover — 7 frames x 0.139 ms ≈ 1 ms.
- SmartTurn v3.2-cpu classification — 18.0 ms mean, 18.9 ms p95 (4 CPU threads). Endpoint compute measured in situ at 46-64 ms including feature prep.
- Qwen3-ASR-1.7B offline pass — 90 ms (1.4 s utterance) / 321 ms (3.9 s) / 413 ms (6.3 s) / 694 ms (8.9 s). p90: 137 / 784 / 478 / 943 ms.

Composed end-to-end, "last speech sample → transcript in hand":
  3.9 s utterance → 611 ms
  6.3 s utterance → 648 ms
  8.9 s utterance → 934 ms

Against the 2.0 s target this hands the rest of the pipeline 1.07-1.39 s for LLM TTFT + TTS TTFA. Against the 3.0 s ceiling there is real slack.

Two things that move these numbers:
- Cold start is 11.8 s (weight load + first inference). Warm the process at boot and keep it resident; never pay this in a turn.
- The p90 tail is the risk, not the p50 (784 ms on a 3.9 s clip). It is contention, and it will get worse when a local LLM and TTS share the same Metal device. Levers, in order: 8-bit quantization (~1.32x, quality-neutral on clean English), drop to 0.6B (−130 to −234 ms per turn), move ASR to the ANE via FluidAudio (removes the contention entirely).

For comparison on identical clips and conditions: Qwen3-ASR-0.6B 63/191/239/460 ms; Parakeet TDT 0.6b v3 32/72/149/111 ms.
memory_gb:
Measured with mx.get_active_memory() / mx.get_peak_memory() on this machine.

- Qwen3-ASR-1.7B fp16 (MLX): **4.08 GB steady resident, 8.16 GB transient peak.** The peak is encoder activations on the longest clip; it returns to 4.08 GB between turns.
- Silero VAD v5 ONNX: 2.3 MB on disk, negligible RSS, CPU only.
- SmartTurn v3.2-cpu ONNX: 8.7 MB on disk, negligible RSS, CPU only.

**Total hearing stack: ~4.1 GB resident, ~8.2 GB peak — 6.4 % of 128 GB.** Memory is a non-issue here, which is precisely the constraint that forced the reference author onto the 0.6B on his 16 GB machine. That constraint does not transfer.

For sizing alternatives on the same measurements: Qwen3-ASR-0.6B 1.57 GB active / 3.14 GB peak; Parakeet TDT 0.6b v3 1.30 GB active / 3.52 GB peak.

Disk: Qwen3-ASR-1.7B weights 4.4 GB (2 safetensors shards), 0.6B 1.8 GB, Parakeet 2.3 GB.
install_commands: # --- environment (Python 3.12; mlx-qwen3-asr requires >=3.10; python3.14 is too new for the ecosystem) ---
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv-asr
uv pip install --python .venv-asr/bin/python mlx-qwen3-asr==0.4.0 onnxruntime numpy huggingface_hub
# optional, only if you also want the Parakeet fallback benchmarked in this report:
uv pip install --python .venv-asr/bin/python parakeet-mlx==0.5.2
# --- small models: fine over HuggingFace, they are tiny ---
HF_HUB_DISABLE_XET=1 .venv-asr/bin/hf download pipecat-ai/smart-turn-v3 --local-dir ./models/smart-turn-v3   # 87 MB, use smart-turn-v3.2-cpu.onnx
HF_HUB_DISABLE_XET=1 .venv-asr/bin/hf download runanywhere/silero-vad-v5 --local-dir ./models/silero-vad-v5   # 2.3 MB
# --- ASR WEIGHTS ARE ALREADY ON THIS MACHINE. Move them, do not re-download. ---

# ModelScope direct with the proxy bypassed measured 7.8 MB/s => ~10 minutes. I used ModelScope.
mkdir -p ./models && mv .cache/research ./models/    # 4.4 GB

# --- NOT NEEDED: torch, transformers, mlx-whisper, whisper.cpp, ollama, cmake. The MLX path has no torch dependency.
# --- If you nonetheless go the transformers route: pip install 'transformers>=5.13' AND you MUST use Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B-hf (see risks).
risks: THE -hf TRAP IS REAL AND SILENT (transformers path only). I verified it from the published weight index: Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B has 708 keys all under `thinker.` (397 `thinker.audio_tower.*`), while transformers 5.x expects `model.audio_tower.*`. from_pretrained does not raise — it warns about newly-initialised weights and hands you a model whose entire audio tower is random. The failure surfaces later as 'Audio features and audio tokens do not match, tokens: 13, features: 13' (counts equal, dimensions not). The configs also differ structurally: non-hf nests under `thinker_config` with audio model_type `qwen3_asr_audio_encoder` and declares transformers_version 4.57.6; -hf is flat with `qwen3_asr_encoder` and 5.13.0.dev0. MITIGATION: use the MLX path, which reads the non-hf layout deliberately and remaps it. If you use transformers anyway, the model id must end in -hf, and assert `not any(k.startswith('thinker.') for k in state_dict)` at load.

SILERO VAD FAILS SILENTLY IF YOU FEED IT 512 SAMPLES. I hit this: the ONNX input is dynamic [B,N], so a bare 512-sample frame runs without error and returns ~0.001 probability on loud speech — total, undetectable failure. At 16 kHz you must feed 576 samples: the previous frame's last 64 samples concatenated with the 512 new ones. The runanywhere card documents none of this. MITIGATION: unit-test the VAD against a clip with known speech boundaries before wiring anything else — mine detected 0.51-4.45 s against a truth of 0.50-4.39 s once corrected.

P90 LATENCY TAIL, NOT P50, IS WHAT WILL BREAK THE BUDGET. Measured p90 for the 1.7B: 784 ms on a 3.9 s utterance, 943 ms on 8.9 s, versus p50 of 321/694. That was with the GPU otherwise idle apart from background system load. Once a local LLM and a TTS model are contending for the same Metal device the tail will get worse, and the 2.0 s target is a p50-shaped goal while user perception is p90-shaped. MITIGATION: measure the composed system, not the components; hold Qwen3-ASR-0.6B (−130 to −234 ms/turn, −0.55 pp accented) and 8-bit quantization (~1.32x) as pre-validated escape hatches; consider moving ASR to the ANE via FluidAudio so it never contends at all.

STREAMING ASR IS NOT PRODUCTION-READY IN mlx-qwen3-asr 0.4.0 — I MEASURED THE CORRUPTION. finalization_mode='latency' gives a beautiful length-independent ~140 ms tail, but the text comes back with seam duplications: 'for teenagers, because. Because education works better', 'The point I am making is that. When you restrict access, you do not. Do not remove the demand.' Both finalization modes. feed_audio() also blocks up to 1151 ms on chunk boundaries, so it cannot live on the audio callback thread. MITIGATION: one offline pass on the VAD-delimited buffer for the authoritative transcript (this is what I benchmarked and what VoxEMW does — his handler yields PartialTranscription for progressive chunks with an explicit comment never to finalise from them). Use streaming only for on-screen interim text, if at all.

HOTWORD INJECTION WILL HALLUCINATE THE LIST INTO UNRELATED SPEECH. The reference author measured this at 10 hotwords: whole-segment recitation of the vocabulary. He cut to 2 and built a runtime detector. The mechanism is structural — hotwords enter the Qwen3 decoder's context as a system prompt, so a longer list both raises the token prior and presents a fluent sequence the LM can continue; on weak acoustic evidence the prior wins. MITIGATION: for an English debate partner use ZERO hotwords — there is no persona jargon to protect and the downside is unbounded. If a proper noun genuinely breaks, add ≤3 rare distinctive terms, gate them off for segments under ~1 s or below an energy floor, add a deterministic post-replace table, and port VoxEMW's is_vocabulary_recitation() guard.

SMART TURN'S ACCENT PROFILE ON L2 ENGLISH IS UNKNOWN. Its English figure (94.26 % accuracy, 3.75 % FPR) comes from 7,820 samples whose accent composition is not published, and much of the training corpus is synthetic (chirp3, orpheus, rime datasets). L2 speakers hesitate differently — longer mid-clause pauses while retrieving vocabulary, which is exactly the pattern the model must classify as 'not finished'. A 3.75 % false-positive rate means roughly 1 turn in 27 gets cut off mid-thought, and that rate could be materially worse for this specific speaker. MITIGATION: log every SmartTurn decision with the audio; raise the analyzer's stop_secs above the 3.0 s default if false cuts appear; the training script and data are open (BSD-2) if fine-tuning on the user's own hesitation patterns becomes worthwhile.

WITHOUT ECHO CANCELLATION THE SYSTEM WILL INTERRUPT ITSELF FOREVER. Speakers plus an always-listening VAD is a feedback loop: the AI's own voice triggers speech_start, which cancels its own reply, whose tail triggers again. MITIGATION, in order: (1) headphones eliminate the problem entirely and are the correct answer for a single-user practice app; (2) getUserMedia echoCancellation:true, or AVAudioSession .voiceChat on iOS/macOS for system AEC — VoxEMW shipped exactly this in v1.8.1; (3) a transcript-level echo guard as the second line, because AEC's known failure mode is precisely double-talk. Do NOT solve it by gating the microphone while the AI speaks — that makes barge-in impossible, which is the whole point of a debate partner.

INTERRUPTING MID-REPLY DESYNCHRONISES THE ARGUMENT IF YOU DON'T TRACK WHAT WAS HEARD. Because TTS generates faster than real time, the number of samples fed to the player massively over-states what the user actually heard. If you write the full generated reply back to context, the AI will later reference arguments the user never heard — fatal in a debate, where callbacks to your own prior points are the substance. MITIGATION: count samples actually played (VoxEMW's pacer keeps `_audio_samples_played` separate from `_audio_samples_fed` for exactly this reason), estimate the heard text prefix from that, and write back only the prefix. Read the counter BEFORE flushing the queue.

RAW VAD SPEECH-START IS TOO TRIGGER-HAPPY FOR DEBATE. Argumentative conversation is dense with backchannels — 'yeah', 'right', 'but', 'mm-hm' — and every one of them will kill the AI's sentence if barge-in is wired straight to VAD. MITIGATION: two-tier. Duck the TTS gain on speech_start (fast, cheap, reversible if it was a backchannel); commit to a real interrupt — cancel LLM generation, flush audio, roll back context — only once the ASR partial clears a word gate (Pipecat's MinWordsInterruptionStrategy uses min_words=3). Note this means you need a fast interim transcript during the AI's speech, which is the one place Parakeet's ~70 ms or a streaming model genuinely earns its keep.

IN-FLIGHT ASR FOR A SUPERSEDED TURN MUST BE ABANDONED, NOT AWAITED. When the user barges in during the previous turn's transcription, a naive pipeline will deliver a stale transcript after the new turn has already started. VoxEMW threads turn_id/turn_revision through every message and drops stale results. MITIGATION: carry a monotonically increasing turn id on every ASR request and discard any result whose id is not current; reset streaming state on interrupt if you use the streaming API at all.

MLX 0.32.2 MAY NOT YET EXPLOIT THE M5's NEURAL ACCELERATORS. My measured latencies did not improve by anything like the 2.25x memory-bandwidth ratio between this M5 Max (614 GB/s) and the M4 Pro (273 GB/s) the published mlx-qwen3-asr benchmarks used — implied decode throughput is roughly 40 tok/s where bandwidth alone suggests ~150. This is upside rather than a defect, but do not budget on the assumption that a future MLX release will deliver it.

COLD START IS 11.8 SECONDS. Weight load plus first inference. Any process-per-request or lazy-load design pays this in a live turn. MITIGATION: load and warm the model at boot with a dummy 1 s buffer (VoxEMW's handler does exactly this in warmup()), and keep the process resident for the session's lifetime.
open_questions: What is the actual WER on THIS user's accent? Every number in this report is from public benchmarks or from macOS `say` synthetic speech. The 16.07 % accented figure is an average over 16 accent groups on Qwen's internal dialog-style set and could be materially better or worse for one specific L2 speaker. ACTION: record 20-30 utterances of the user genuinely arguing (not reading), hand-transcribe them, and run Qwen-1.7B / Qwen-0.6B / Parakeet over the set. It is a couple of hours and it settles the single most consequential choice in this component. All three models are already downloaded.

Does SmartTurn v3.2 mis-fire on this user's hesitation pattern? Vocabulary-retrieval pauses in L2 speech are longer and differently shaped than the native pauses that dominate the training data. Measure the false-cut rate over a real session before tuning anything else — and note the fix might be as cheap as raising the analyzer's stop_secs, or as involved as fine-tuning (training code and data are open, BSD-2).

Does 8-bit quantization hold up on ACCENTED audio? Upstream reports 8-bit reproducing fp16 exactly on LibriSpeech test-clean, but clean read English is the easiest possible case and quantization error tends to surface first on the hardest inputs. If 8-bit is quality-neutral on accented speech it is the cleanest ~1.32x win available; if it is not, that is worth knowing before it ships.

How much do ASR, a local LLM and TTS actually contend on one Metal device? Every latency figure here is ASR-alone. The whole system's p90 is what the user experiences, and GPU contention is the most plausible way this design misses its budget. This has to be measured end-to-end, and the answer determines whether FluidAudio's ANE path (ASR off the GPU entirely) is an optimization or a requirement.

Can the streaming seam-duplication be fixed rather than avoided? The measured ~140 ms length-independent tail is a genuinely large win over the 321-694 ms offline pass — it would hide almost all ASR cost inside the user's own speech. The `unfixed_chunk_num` / `unfixed_token_num` prefix-rollback knobs and `endpointing_mode='energy'` are unexplored, and the project is Apache-2.0 with 666 tests. Worth an afternoon before accepting the offline cost permanently.

Is Parakeet's accent weakness real for this speaker, or an artifact of the benchmarks? The 9.74 % Japanese-accented figure comes from a third-party study, not NVIDIA, and Parakeet is 4-8x faster on measured hardware. If it holds up on the user's own audio, it changes the whole latency picture. The head-to-head is the same experiment as the first open question — run them together.

Should Parakeet run alongside Qwen rather than instead of it? At 32-72 ms it is nearly free, and a fast draft transcript during the AI's speech is exactly what the barge-in word-gate needs. This is a plausible best-of-both architecture (Parakeet for interim/interrupt decisions, Qwen for the authoritative turn) that I did not have time to prototype.

Would FluidAudio's Parakeet EOU 120m collapse VAD + SmartTurn + ASR into one ANE model? It is streaming ASR with end-of-utterance detection built in, ~232 MB, running on the Neural Engine. If the app is Swift rather than Python, that is architecturally simpler AND removes GPU contention. English-only, and it inherits Parakeet's accent profile — but the architectural saving may outweigh that.
